Modeling progressed stratigraphically, starting from the oldest (deepest) geologic unit and building upward. Contacts between units were digitized from cross sections, contour maps, and geologic maps. Then contacts were used to automatically generate surface boundaries. Once a surface was created, the corresponding 3D volume for that geologic unit was created, either 15 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. above or below the surface depending on the unit’s classification (e.g., deposit, erosion, or intrusion). All geologic units were modeled as deposits, apart from surficial deposits, which were modeled as erosional features to allow them to cut into the underlying stratigraphy to better reflect their geomorphic character. After generating each surface and corresponding volume, a basic quality control process was applied using criteria as the fits with the input data and geologic response. As part of the model quality control, adjustments were made either by modifying software parameters or through minor manual editing of the surfaces. The finalized 3D geologic model, along with accompanying hydrogeologic property maps, provides a comprehensive synthesis of the available geologic and hydrological data for the SJMA. While simplified, the model offers a representative visualization of the region’s subsurface geology and supports the interpretation of its geologic evolution. At the base of the model lie highly deformed, undifferentiated volcaniclastic and igneous basement rocks, formed in a subduction-related volcanic arc. These basement units represent the island’s geologic core. After the cessation of volcanic activity, thick sequences of siliciclastic and carbonate sediments were deposited in shallow marine environments along Puerto Rico’s northern and southern coasts. Subsequent northward tilting uplifted these sedimentary units above sea level along the North Coast, resulting in a gentle dip of approximately 4°–5° to the north and an overall east- west regional strike. Figure 10 shows an oblique, southwest-facing view of the complete 3D model, illustrating the spatial relationships among the major geologic units. Hydrogeologically, the SJMA features are both confined; these units are overlain by the clay-rich Cibao Formation, which acts as an effective confining layer. At the surface, surficial deposits form the uppermost 10–30 m of the subsurface. These deposits exhibit high spatial variability in both composition and water-bearing capacity across the SJMA, influencing groundwater recharge and flow dynamics. 16 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications.
